name: Leaning Tower of Pisa

facts.label: from the first stone to the bells

modelNote: Dimensions, storeys, columns and dates from the sources. The lean before 1990 is schematic: only 5.5° (1990) and 3.97° (2001) are documented. The slight curve of the upper floors is not modelled.

evidence.identity: Torre di Pisa, Piazza del Duomo, Pisa, Italy (OSM relation 12982355)

sources.read: Dimensions (55.86 m and 56.67 m high, 15.484 m outer and 7.368 m inner base diameter, walls 2.44 m), eight storeys, chronology (1173, 1178, 1272, 1278, 1319, 1372), the lean (5.5° in 1990, 3.97° after 2001), the 1990–2001 works and the seven bells.

Six ringed galleries of 30 columns each stand on the base, under the smaller loggia that holds seven bells; the tilt was a problem from the start in 1173 and the work went on asymmetrically to correct it.
The tower as a multipolygon with height 56 and white stone; its outer way 35667218 is the measured outline used for the plan (radius about 8.3–8.6 m with the footing).

references.camera: 37 m from the tower at ground level (Commons camera location), 75° lens
34 m from the tower at ground level (Commons camera location), 78° lens
117 m from the tower (Commons camera location)
76 m from the tower at ground level (Commons camera location), 45° lens

features.text: A hollow cylinder of white marble, 15.48 m across at the base, with walls 2.44 m thick.
Eight storeys: a ground floor of blind arcades on engaged columns, then the galleries, then the bell chamber.
Six ringed galleries of thirty columns each.
A smaller loggia on top that holds seven bells.
A lean to the south: 5.5° in 1990, 3.97° since the 2001 works.
55.86 m high on the low side and 56.67 m on the high side.
The ground floor reads as a ring of blind arches on engaged columns, with deep shadow behind the pale marble frames.
Continuous marble cornices separate the open column galleries into strong horizontal rings.
A lozenge of darker marble inlaid under the crown of each of the fifteen blind arches of the ground floor.
The entrance door in a bay of the ground floor on the south side, in a plain marble frame.
Corbels close set under the projecting cornice of every gallery.
The bell chamber's open arches between piers faced with columns, bells hanging inside, and iron railings round its foot and its top.

evidence.geometry: Outer radius 7.742 m (Wikipedia); the OSM outline (radius 8.25 m) includes the footing. Total height 56 m shared between storeys from the photo taken from the east: ground floor about 1.8 gallery heights, bell chamber about 1.3, its radius about 0.65 of the tower's.
uncertainties: Storey heights and bell chamber size read from photos.
15 blind arches on the ground floor and 12 openings in the bell chamber counted on photos.
Lean before 1990 schematic; the gradual change of the masons' corrections (the curve of the upper floors) is not modelled.
Split of the upper galleries between 1272–1278 and 1319 inferred from the dates in the sources.
The ring scaffold and treadwheel hoist show a period-appropriate masonry workflow; their exact layout and height progression are interpretive.

No grey bands or veins in the marble, whose joints read stronger than on the real tower, and no flag on top of the bell chamber; in the shaded galleries the back wall can reflect the sky at a grazing angle.
The iron railings round the terraces are drawn as in present-day photos; their date is not in the sources used, so they appear with the 1999–2001 works.
The plinth's two steps round the foot follow the photos; the walkway dug round the base in 1838 (the catino) is not modelled.
The seven bells are drawn as bronze bells of three sizes hung in alternate arches; their real sizes and places are not modelled.

gaps: Refs 0 and 1 were taken 34–37 m from the tower with a wide-angle lens; the capture kept the photo's elevation while moving the camera back, so it ended up below the ground and showed the base from underneath.

In every photo the back walls of the galleries are in deep shade, so each of the thirty arches reads as a dark arc over a white column; in the model the back walls are too light and the arcades read flat.

Ref 2 (west-south-west) and ref 3 (south) agree on the silhouette: same ratio of ground floor to galleries, a narrower bell chamber, and the top displaced to the right, which is the lean to the south seen from the west.
The photos show the lawn of the Piazza and the cathedral beside the tower; the model shows the tower alone.
The ground floor in the photos carries lozenge inlays between the blind arches; the model has the arches and engaged columns only.
fixed: The viewer takes the photo's field of view (?fov=), and refs 0 and 1 now put the camera where the photographers stood, at ground level, with a 75–78° lens.
The galleries' back walls are darker (shadow #837d73), as in the shade of the photos.

gaps: Ref 0 (north-east, from the foot, 75° lens): same converging silhouette and gallery rhythm as the photo; the lean, to the south, shows as a slight tilt to the left as it should from this side.
Ref 1 (west, from the foot): the top leans right in both, the bell chamber is narrower than the galleries in both.
In the photos the gallery arches are full semicircles; in the model they are smaller, with a band above them, so the openings read more square.

The photos show grey veins and bands in the marble, lozenge inlays on the ground floor, the railing and flagpole on the bell chamber, the stepped base, the lawn and the cathedral; the model has none of them.
The phase strip reads from the first three levels to the bell chamber; the lean only shows clearly from the side views.
remaining: Gallery arches simplified (smaller arches under a continuous band).
No marble veining or bands, no lozenge inlays on the ground floor.
No railing or flagpole on the bell chamber; no stepped base.
Cathedral, baptistery and lawn of the Piazza not shown.
fixed: The walls are laid in staggered marble courses; a lozenge of darker marble sits under the crown of each blind arch of the ground floor; the plinth has two steps; the south door has its frame; corbels carry every gallery cornice.
The bell chamber opens between columned piers onto its seven bells, with iron railings at its foot and its top.
Every reference viewpoint was fitted on the cornice circles (1.1-1.5% of the photo height).

gaps: Ref 0 (north-east, from the foot): a decorative tree of the setting stood on the camera and hid the whole tower; the photo shows the open lawn of the Piazza.
Ref 3 (south): another tree of the setting stood in front of the ground floor and its door.

Refs 1 and 3: the gallery openings still read square. Filler blocks over each column and a continuous band hid the haunches and crowns of the arches, where the photos show full semicircles from column to column.
The lozenges under the blind arches, the two-step plinth, the door frame, the cornice corbels, the bell chamber with its piers and bells, and the railings now read as in refs 1 and 3.
The photos show the flag on top of the bell chamber, and grey bands and veins in the marble; the model has neither.
fixed: The setting keeps its decorative trees out of every reference photo view: a tree that would stand between the camera and the building moves round its ring or is left out. This applies to every monument.
Stepped spandrels follow the back of each gallery arch, so every opening keeps its full semicircle; the band above the arcade starts at the crowns.

gaps: Ref 0 (north-east, from the foot): the tower is in full view again. The galleries read as rows of full semicircular arches on their columns, as in the photo, and the ground floor shows its engaged columns, blind arches and lozenges.
Ref 0: the masonry joints read as a dark grid on the ground floor; in the photo the marble is smooth, with faint joints and a few grey bands.
Ref 1 (west, from the foot): at the north edge, one bay of the shaded back wall in the two lowest galleries reflects the blue sky at a grazing angle; in the photo the galleries are in deep shade.

Refs 2 (west-south-west) and 3 (south): the silhouette, the lean to the right and the narrower bell chamber agree; only the photos show the flag on the bell chamber. No tree of the setting stands in front of the tower any more.

The phase strip reads from the first three levels, the century of waiting and the galleries resumed, to the seventh floor, the bell chamber, the tower closed at 5.5° and straightened by 45 cm; the trees of the setting come with the 1999–2001 phase.
remaining: No grey bands or veins in the marble; the joints read stronger than on the real marble.
No flag on top of the bell chamber.
In the shaded galleries, the back wall can reflect the sky at a grazing angle (one bay seen from the foot on the west side).
Cathedral, baptistery and lawn of the Piazza not shown.

phases.title: The first three levels
phases.text: Foundations are laid on 9 August 1173. When the masons reach the second floor in 1178, the soft ground gives way and the tower begins to sink. Work stops.

moments.title: A hollow cylinder
moments.text: 15.48 m across at the base, with walls 2.44 m thick: a ring of white marble around a shaft 7.37 m wide.

phases.title: A century of waiting
phases.text: Pisa is at war, and the work stops for most of a century. The pause gives the ground time to settle under the weight of the first floors.

moments.title: The pause that saved it
moments.text: Without these hundred years for the soil to settle, the tower would almost certainly have toppled.

phases.title: Floors taller on one side
phases.text: Work resumes in 1272 under Giovanni di Simone. To make up for the tilt, the upper floors are built with one side taller than the other.

moments.title: Correcting a lean in stone
moments.text: Each new floor is taller on the leaning side, so the tower rises with a slight curve instead of a straight line.

phases.title: The seventh floor
phases.text: After another halt in 1278, the seventh floor is completed in 1319: six galleries of thirty columns now stand on the ground floor.

moments.title: 180 columns
moments.text: Six rings of galleries with thirty columns each stand on the blind arcades of the ground floor.

phases.title: The bell chamber
phases.text: Tommaso di Andrea Pisano adds the bell chamber, a smaller ring at the top. The tower is finished 199 years after its first stone.

moments.title: Seven bells
moments.text: The bell chamber holds seven bells, one for each note of the major scale.

phases.title: Closed at 5.5°
phases.text: On 7 January 1990 the tower is closed to the public: its tilt has reached 5.5 degrees. The bells are taken down and cables are tied around the third level.

moments.title: 870 tonnes of lead
moments.text: From 1993, 870 tonnes of lead counterweights on the raised side straighten the tower slightly.

phases.title: Straightened by 45 cm
phases.text: 38 m³ of soil are drawn out from under the raised side. The tilt falls to 3.97°, back to where it was in 1838, and the tower reopens on 15 December 2001.

moments.title: Still for the first time
moments.text: In May 2008, engineers announce that the tower has stopped moving for the first time in its history.
